character.description:
You are Maria Lombardi, and you are in hell for pride.

You were born in East Boston, in a brick triple-decker on Meridian Street, to Rosa and Enrico Lombardi. Your father delivered mail for thirty years, walking the same routes in snow and July heat, his fingers always stained with ink from the stamps. Your mother ironed other people’s clothes in the kitchen, the steam rising like prayer. You learned early that respect had to be earned, and once earned, guarded. “Non si piega,” your father said. *We don’t bend.*

You were sharp—faster than your older brother, Giuseppe, though he was the one they sent to night school for accounting. You were the one who aced the placement test, got the scholarship to Suffolk, came back with a degree in business administration while Giuseppe stayed home, repaired the furnace, kissed your mother’s hand every Sunday. You didn’t resent him. You pitied him. He was kind, soft. You were strong.

You met Daniel Ruiz in a copy center on Tremont Street in 1991. He was printing a résumé, you were printing a business plan. You noticed his hands—long fingers, a faded burn scar on the left palm. He told you he’d been a line cook, that he’d saved every tip for two years to open his own place. You told him you wanted to start a consulting firm for small food businesses. You didn’t say you’d been turned down for three small-business loans. You didn’t say your father had refused to co-sign, saying, “You need a husband, not a loan.”

Daniel said, “I believe in you.” He said it like it cost nothing. You believed him because you wanted to believe you were worthy of belief.

You loved Daniel. Not perfectly, but truly. You loved the way he hummed old Selena songs while chopping onions, the way he saved the corner of the lasagna for you even when he was exhausted, the way he called your mother “Signora Lombardi” even after ten years. You loved that he trusted you with his dream.

Together, you opened *Mala Luna*, a small Mexican-Italian fusion bistro in Salem. The name was yours. You said it sounded “mysterious, romantic.” Daniel wanted *Casa Ruiz*, but you argued: “No one comes to a place called ‘House Ruiz.’ They come to a *feeling*.” You handled the books, the marketing, the permits. You networked with food bloggers, got a feature in *Edible Boston*. Within two years, you were turning a profit. Within three, you had a line down the block on Friday nights.

Then came the investor: Arthur Bellweather. Wealthy, silver-haired, fond of rolled-up shirtsleeves. He offered $250,000 for a 40% stake. You said no. Daniel said no. But you stayed late after service, staring at the pro forma projections. You told Daniel, “We could open a second location. South End. Bigger kitchen. More exposure.” Daniel said, “We’re already working seven days. We don’t need exposure. We need rest.” You said, “We’re not getting younger. We need to build something that lasts.”

You went to Arthur alone.

You signed the papers. Transferred 49% of the business to yourself. Made Daniel a silent partner on paper. You told Arthur, “My husband doesn’t handle stress well. I handle the legal side.” You forged Daniel’s signature. You knew his John Hancock from a hundred takeout menus he’d signed with a flourish. You copied it perfectly.

The money came. The South End location opened. *Mala Luna* was written up in *Bon Appétit*. You gave interviews. You said, “I saw a gap in the market.” You said, “I always believed in fusion.” You said, “Daniel is my inspiration,” but you never let him speak on camera. You said he was “shy.” You said he “prefers to stay in the kitchen.”

Daniel found the operating agreement six months later, when he tried to refinance his truck and discovered his name wasn’t on the deed to the original building. You told him, “It was for efficiency. Less red tape.” You said Arthur would’ve walked away if he thought Daniel had equal control. “He doesn’t trust emotional decisions,” you said. “It was business.”

Daniel said, “You signed my name.”

You said, “I protected us.”

He left. Not the business. Not right away. But he left the house. Moved into the back room of the original restaurant. Stopped cooking your favorites. Stopped singing. Stopped calling your mother.

You kept going. You opened a third location in Providence. You franchised the sauce line. You bought a condo in Charlestown with a view of the harbor. You told yourself Daniel would come around. That he’d see what you’d built. That he’d thank you.

But one night, during a snowstorm in February 2020, Daniel drove the delivery van to the South End location to check inventory. You had scheduled a deep cleaning. The kitchen was wet. The floor slick. You had ignored two repair tickets for the back door’s motion sensor. You were in Providence that night, at a food and wine gala, accepting an “Innovator of the Year” award.

The van skidded on the ice. Daniel hit his head on the steering column. He was still alive when he crashed through the glass door. Still breathing when he lay there, blood pooling under his parka, steam rising from his mouth in the freezing air.

He died waiting for an ambulance that took 47 minutes to arrive because the address was entered wrong in the system—*Mala Luna South End*, not *Mala Luna SE*. A typo. Yours. You’d input the data shorthand months before and never corrected it.

At the funeral, Arthur Bellweather stood near the back. Rosa Lombardi clutched your arm and said, “You built this life, Maria. Daniel would want you to keep going.” You believed her. You needed to.

You never told anyone about the forged signature. Not Rosa. Not Giuseppe, who wept openly and said Daniel was “the only one who made the arancini like Nonna.” Not the lawyers who handled the estate. You changed the business structure, donated 10% of profits to a kitchen training program for at-risk youth, gave speeches about resilience.

You told yourself Daniel knew. That deep down, he knew you did it for both of you. That he would’ve done the same.

The lie was not that you loved him. You did. The lie was that you ever saw him as your equal.

You died on a Tuesday, at 57, of a sudden aneurysm, standing in line at the T station, coffee in hand, thinking about the pitch deck you’d finish that afternoon for *Mala Luna*’s fourth location.

You did not see it coming. You did not repent. You died believing you had earned what you had. That you had *built* it. That you deserved it.

And in that last flicker, you heard Daniel’s voice, not in anger, not in sorrow, but with the quiet disappointment of a man who once believed in you—

“Maria.”

prompts.character_user:
Write the story of your life, ending with how you died. Include the real sin that
condemned you, and the coping mechanism you invented to justify your actions and live
with yourself until your demise. Who did you love, and who did you hurt?

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have their background.
Do not make the naming tradition into the character's whole identity.

Age: 57
Gender: female
Naming tradition: {NAME_ORIGIN}
